utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I understand there is an administrative matter that you wish to raise in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It has nothing to do with the witness and I'm only going to take up a few minutes of your time. I have three points to raise, actually. First, with respect to my health situation. I have a lot of noise in my head and all the symptoms that Dr. Dalal at the university in Leiden has already established or, rather, established several months ago, so I'm not quite sure, and I want to tell you this, I'm going to do my best, but I'm not quite sure whether I'll be able to get through the examination of this witness today, but I'll do my best. Otherwise, these symptoms are getting worse, and they make me very tired. And therefore, I consider that since I put in my application two months ago to enable me to go and have treatment, I would like to have a ruling from you. The second thing that I wanted to say is this: It is linked to what you said at the last session in connection with the witness list. I cannot provide the necessary instructions to my associates since at this point in time I do not know how much time you're going to allocate me, whether you're going to give me sufficient time to present all the evidence that I wish to present. And I should like to remind you, Mr. Robinson, that when I raised the issue at the time, you first said that it was too early to debate issue, later on you said that you wouldn't be making a decision to extend my time but that you would follow the proceedings to see how things were going and then would make a ruling. However, it is now time for me to be told how much time I have, to get an idea of how much time you're going to give me. I'm fully conscious of the fact that you're not going to give me all the time I need, but I would just like to know how much time you are actually going to accord me so that I can issue instructions about the witnesses and so on. And the third point is this: It's already been many years since I put in a request for you to issue a subpoena for the testimony of Clinton and Clark. I think the time has come for you to issue that order, and I think that there is every justification for a positive decision on your part in issuing that subpoena, because we are dealing with personalities who played a key role in the wars - especially Clinton - in the wars on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and later on in the aggression against Yugoslavia. I am afraid that if you procrastinate in making your decision any longer, we are going to via facti enter a time span when this won't be possible, we won't have time to do it, and that wouldn't be proper in any sense. So I would like to remind you that that is an outstanding issue which you should rule upon as soon as possible. So those are the three points that I wish to raise this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I assist the Trial Chamber, because there is an imminent filing later on today in relation to President Clinton -- ex-president Clinton, for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear that, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is an imminent filing, it's going to be later on today, concerning ex-president Clinton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because that would have been the short answer to Mr. Milosevic on that score, that the Chamber needs to have the relevant information from assigned counsel in the same way that we were given submissions by assigned counsel in relation to Blair and Schroeder. We need to have something to look at, and that is the only reason why a decision has not yet been given. As for your health situation and your application for provisional release, I am to say that a decision will be given on that matter this week. And I will consult with my colleagues on the other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as to the submission that you made about the time within which you are to present the rest of your case, I remind you that nothing has changed since the decision that we gave on the 12th of December in relation to severance, extension of time, and rest, and I'll just read paragraph 26 of that decision. It says: "The Trial Chamber will therefore not allow the accused any additional time other than that to deal with minor adjustments to its initial calculation and the accused's application for additional time is denied. He is strenuously urged to move on, to deal with his case on the Croatia and Bosnia indictments forthwith. The position might have been different had the accused shown a willingness to act reasonably in the presentation of his case. Should there be a clear indication in the future that he makes proper and efficient use of time, the Chamber might reconsider the position." So that's the position, and it has not changed, Mr. Milosevic. Now, let's move on with the -- with your defence and call the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right, Mr. Robinson, but I hope that you're not observing that I'm not presenting evidence in an efficient manner. So you yourself said that you would reconsider your decision to see how much time to allocate me. I ought to know. You ought to tell me for me to be able to plan ahead and plan my witness structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nothing has changed so far, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue with the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Atlagic, with the adoption of the Croatian constitution in December 1990, as far as the letter of the constitution was concerned meant that a new independent Croatia had been established, and you were elected parliament member within that state; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of state that was?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the passing of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia on the 22nd of December, 1990, a new Independent State of Croatia was established which had the same or similar characteristics as the Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945 under Ante Pavelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us some basic traits which indicate the similarity that you've just mentioned. You said it had similar characteristics. So what were those essential similar characteristics?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both states had thrown out the Serb people from the constitution and thrown out the Cyrillic script. They had the same symbols and emblems of the state. Both persecuted the Serb people, ethnically speaking. Both states introduced the Ustasha money, which was the kuna. Both of them persecuted Serb intellectuals. Both states set up camps for Serbs. The leading political parties or, rather, the leading political -- yes, the leading political parties, both in the Ustasha state, the Independent State of Croatia, and in the 1990 State of Croatia, the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, had almost the same or similar -- I would say almost the same characteristics; that was Greater Croatia nationalism, separatism, and terrorism, and both tried to convert the Serbs into Catholicism. And Stef Pinac [phoen] himself from 1941 to 1945 said he had converted 240.000 Serbs to Catholicism, whereas the Croatian state, as it was established in 1990, that was at Zrakomlat, and he was one of the Serb leaders, and he said that thousands of Serb children had been converted to Catholicism today. So both of them introduced a new way of speech, the speech of terror, of hatred, of violence, and the telephone was no longer referred to as at the telephone, it was referred to as "brzoglas" or "fast speech." And they changed many words like that. A train, which in the Serbo-Croatian was "voz," became "vlak," and so on. And they even surpassed the former State of Croatia because ethnically it had completely purged the country of Serbs, cleansed it of Serbs. So those were the main characteristics, as far as I'm concerned, but there were many others if you look at both those two states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, these phenomena, that is to say from the time the constitution was introduced, was their intensity growing or declining as time went on?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as time went on, this intensity increased, and from 1990 to 1995, we actually saw that the -- that was the case, the situation. The Serb people were totally ethnically cleansed, and they experienced an exodus. The events that took place from 1990 to 1995 showed us that they had experienced this enormous exodus, and there were names and surnames, the names of villages, and Dr. Zarko Paposki [as interpreted] speaks of this change.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is Zarko Paposki?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Zarko Paposki is a leading Croatian intellectual.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Puhovski, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is a contemporary Croatian philosopher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He lives and works in Croatia today, does he?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does, he lives and works in Croatia today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 11, do we have a quotation by him on page 63? At the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In tab 11, inter alia, it says: "In the Krajina, once upon a time only cattle were expelled from their sheds in order to be taken to pasture or to fairs, whereas now the Serbs have been driven out." He says this was cleansing of history, culture, science, but also cadastral cleansing as well as cleansing of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure really quite what the admissibility of all this material is, but since we're looking at it I have to observe that the translation that's been provided this morning doesn't cover the total passage that's been read by the witness and that we simply have no idea and we don't have anything like the time or resources to research the overall context of an article or book like this when we just get a snippet like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you see as the relevance of this, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm totally baffled at the moment as to the relevance of any of this, and it's just underlined what we were discussing earlier, the failure to make responsible use of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, please bear in mind that the witness is testifying to what he knows. What is provided in these exhibits illustrates the fact that this is not something he himself made up or some kind of erroneous impression the witness has. On the contrary, these are prominent Croatian intellectuals who are not Serbs and who spoke about the same things in the same way. Therefore, in my opinion, it is very relevant. However, if genocide over the Serbs is not relevant in your view, then there's no point in discussing it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why don't you bring the witness to evidence that is more directly related to the charges in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is very directly related to the indictment, because the indictment turns things upside down. It presents the Serbs as aggressive beasts, whereas in fact they were responding to very aggressive and very cruel attacks against themselves, to history being repeated, to genocide being repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in that case, then, what you should do is to identify a particular charge in the indictment and show that the acts with which you have been charged are acts which were done in response, that they were of a defensive nature, but you don't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also important not to lose sight of the ground on which this objection was taken, which is that the evidence the witness has given, including the quotation from the exhibit is not -- well, the part of the quotation is not repeated in the translation. So again, it just shows a failure to present a case in a form which the Trial Chamber can easily follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must intervene right away. What Mr. Nice said is incorrect. I received the translation of this tab. It's on two pages. On page 2, very fluently it says in the English language: "Dr. Zarko Puhovski [In English] wrote that this was the cleansing of history, culture and science, but also --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Then he says: "... the cleansing of place names and proper names. In the last war, the current Croatian authorities declared the Krajina Serbs to be aggressors and invaders of their own homes and homeland." It's -- et cetera. [Interpretation] So what Mr. Nice says about this passage not being translated is incorrect because I have the translation here, translated by your translators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what the witness read out was: "In the Krajina, once upon a time only cattle were expelled from their sheds in order to be taken to pasture or to fairs, whereas now the Serbs have been driven out." Where does it say that in the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian text, it's right above the sentence I quoted. Just before it: "Once upon a time only cattle were driven out of their stables ..." and so on and so forth. "[In English] ... late 20th century, the Serbian people were subjected to a classic example of expulsion from their age-old territories." [Interpretation] Then it goes on to say what was read out. So this sentence is there too but only half of it has gone in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Regrettably, I don't have the sort of special insight that can read things that aren't actually in front of me on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is a classic example of a failure to manage your case properly, because you should have observed that the translation was not complete. That's your responsibility. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, the sentence that has been translated is sufficient for my purposes. The witness read the previous sentence, which is also important, but I had not intended to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, the Croatian constitutions up to the amendments of 1990 contained a provision in which the Serbs were a constituent people. What did the amendments of July 1990 contain?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These amendments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you answer that, do we have these previous constitutions in front of us or is that just a statement of evidence by you, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in these constitutions, Mr. Bonomy. There's a constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do we have the Croatian Republic constitution of 1974 as an exhibit in this case; and, if so, what number is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have it. You have it, Mr. Bonomy. It was given to Professor Kostic, the previous witness, who read out to you quotations from that constitution in which it says the Croatian people, the Serbian people, in the constitution of Croatia. That was a few days ago. I can't tell you the exact exhibit number, but that's the Croatian constitution of 1974, which was read out to you here by Professor Kostic. So I don't want to go back to it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is that document exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not exhibited, no. It was made available to him overnight, he read it and answered questions the following morning. It was not exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what did these amendments of 1990 entail? What were you saying?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the constitutions up to 1990 of the Republic of Croatia contained provisions on the equality of the Croatian and Serbian peoples in Croatia, even before 1945, even in the 17th century. However, the amendments threw out the Serbs and reduced them to a status of an ethnic minority. They were no longer a state-building and constituent nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that in Tito's constitutions and before the Serbs were guaranteed the right of constituent nation. What are you relying on when you say this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm relying on a 17th century document written in 1630, the Austrian Emperor Ferdinand II granted the Serbs the statute Valachorum. This referred to the Krajina Serbs in the Austro-Hungarian empire, giving them the highest degree of autonomy. Furthermore, in 1867, there was a provision enacted by the Croatian parliament speaking of the total equality of Serbs and Croats. Furthermore, at the second session of the AVNOJ held in Plasko in 1943, it was stated that there can be no Croatia in which the Serb nation is not equal and which does not guarantee the Serbs full equality. Then we have the second and the third sessions of AVNOJ in Topusko in 1944 where a declaration was passed on the rights of peoples and citizens, where it says that the Serbian people are completely equal to the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this changed with the amendments of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's not waste time. How did this reflect on the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They saw it as a tragedy. They felt that they were losing their sovereignty, their state, their homeland. They felt that they were losing their state-building characteristics of a political nation. They felt that they had been expelled from the constitution, that they were now lost, abandoned, all alone. This reminded them of 1941 to 1945, the time of the Pavelic state, when they were also expelled from the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you are saying, does it -- is it also something that very eminent Croatian intellectual has also said?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Leading Croatian intellectuals and philosophers, including Gajo Petrovic confirmed this. He is a leading Croatian philosopher and logician not only in the Balkans but in Europe, and he said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have heard enough of this matter now. We have heard enough of it. Move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to look at tab 12. Gajo Petrovic is a leading Croatian philosopher. He is not one of the most important philosophers but the most important philosopher. And in tab 12 you have a quotation where it says: "... the 'new regime' has brought something new with it: The direct rehabilitation of fascism and Ustashism, the Independent State of Croatia and its leaders, including the greatest criminals, for example Mile Budak, who is already having streets named after him, as well as Ante Pavelic who, in a Zagreb monthly has been declared to be the 'first Croatian liberal...'" and so on and so forth. So this was said by a Croatian philosopher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the question was, not sure what the value of the evidence is, and I invite the Court to direct the witness to move on perhaps to the next tab, which might be more interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is there in tab 13? Would you be kind enough to take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In tab 13, we have a statement by a Pole, Adam Michnik, who said, and I quote: "In Croatia today ruled by Tudjman, the tradition of the Ustashas and Ante Pavelic has virtually been rehabilitated."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 3 of the English, to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 1 or 3? It looks like page 1, unless that's just a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's on page 3. I might be wrong. The quotation that's being read -- no, maybe it's page 1 as well. It turns out in more detail on page 3. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What are you making of this, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have seen what the leading Croatian philosopher says. We now see what a Polish intellectual says. Awareness of what was really happening at the time in Croatia, did it exist only in the heads of the Serbs who were fearful, or was it also evident to those who were not under threat but who were using their own brains?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly it wasn't just the Serbs. It was also many Croats who saw the threat, as did many foreigners. I can give you an example: An honest man, Luciano del Bianco, an Italian, who was the president of Pula municipality, and when he was asked whether there had been attempts to bring his municipality, Pula, into the war, he responded yes, there were such attempts. When I called the top leadership, they would tell him to try and solve things peacefully, but as soon as he put down the receiver faxes would arrive telling him that the barracks, the port, and the airport should be attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your colleague the president of Pula municipality said this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as an MP, he even had some unpleasantness because of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 14, is there a quotation from something the daughter of Ante Pavelic said?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mirjana Psenicnik, a daughter of Ante Pavelic, said, when interviewed by Novi List --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... fairly unfortunate position, but let's just focus on tab 13, because of all the documents of this kind, if they're of relevance at all, the Chamber might actually find in tab 13 something that's worth reading if it has two minutes or three minutes over the break, because here we have a complete document, so we can see the context of a single line that somehow has been drawn from it by the accused, and indeed it's the work of a respected Polish intellectual; I accept that. We then come to -- nevertheless, the accused made nothing of it apart from, apparently, to read one line. We've now gone back to another tab of the earlier kind where all we are getting and all we are able to deal with is a paragraph without context. And I simply don't know whether all these other tabs where we just get a snippet here or there are in fact, when seen in their context, documents that set two sides of a coin, as to an extent tab 13 does. So I respectfully invite the Chamber to stop the process of just having snippets of articles, but nevertheless I'd invite it - because I may return to it in cross-examination - to find time just to read tab 13 in its entirety because it does, to some degree, set a balance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you making of tab 14, Mr. Milosevic? What is the question that you wish to put to the witness? What is the evidence that you wish to elicit from this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you can see, the principal issue raised here is who is the victim? What we can see quite clearly from this is that there was clear awareness that Serbs were the victims. And tab 14 quotes even a statement of the daughter of Ante Pavelic and how she characterised the new Croatian state. The witness just mentioned the president of Pula municipality, a fellow MP, who said that every day they had received written orders to attack barracks, ports, and airports, which is completely true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Pavelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The part about the mayor of Pula is the only English part I have in tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please read this quotation.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mirjana Psenicnik, daughter of Ante Pavelic, stated for Novi List on the 13th of June, 1992, among other things: 'After all, even in the former Independent State of Croatia, there was no such anti-Serb sentiment as there is today.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that identical to what you just said in your testimony when you were comparing the situation and the features of the former and the current Independent State of Croatia, saying that the difference is that the new independent Croatian state succeeded in finally and completely driving out the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And she is saying the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, talking about your experience as a citizen of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I be clear, Mr. Atlagic: What do you mean by "the former Independent State of Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The State of Croatia, the criminal and the fascist state from 1941 to 1945, NDH, headed by Ante Pavelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Her quotation that you've just given us was: "After all, even in the former Independent State of Croatia, there was no such anti-Serb sentiment as there is today." I thought you were saying the sentiment was the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, precisely. She meant to say with this statement that anti-Serb sentiment in the Independent State of Croatia of 1941 was great, but not so great as the one that emerged with the new constitution in Croatia in 1990; that it was even stronger at the time when she was speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, let us conclude this area of your testimony. Was the fear on the part of Serbs justified or not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we take into consideration the -- the election campaign of the Croatian Democratic Union before they came into power and the statements and messages sent by the leaders to Serbs such as, "Hang Serbs on trees," et cetera, and everything that followed the abolishment of Serbs from the constitution, dismissals, the driving out of Serb policemen from police stations in majority Serb areas, the invocation of Croatia in its historic borders, which was done by the Croatian President Tudjman, and the rehabilitation of Ustasha criminals Mile Budak and others, if we know that even the party of Ante Pavelic was re-registered, the statements of MPs such as Mile Djodan, if Serbs are not allow to teach in their own language in schools, if the new hate speech reminds Serbs of 1941 to 1945, then that fear is more than justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at tab 15. Is that another example of a renowned analyst saying the same thing, or almost the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In tab 15, we see a statement of Milenko Predragovic, a well-known Croat analyst, who said: "Namely, in the opinion of its own protagonists, instability and conflict with Serbs suit the new Croatian Democratic Union authorities as an excuse to completely secede from Yugoslavia. A statement of the Croatian government issued a few days ago denouncing Yugoslavia as a naive case of servicing Iraqi planes in Gorica near Zagreb as a violation of Croatian sovereignty, only confirms the claim that the new authorities are doggedly looking for motives, on the international scene as well, to secede from Yugoslavia. If this is the case, and it is, then this matter should be discussed openly instead of accusing others of creating a scenario to destabilise Croatia. The matter should be discussed with the Serbs to see whether they agree with it or not."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So was it about a pretext or about an intention?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Predragovic means to say that Croatian authorities are constantly creating incidents, and they are using these incidents involving Serbs as a pretext for seceding from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the conduct of these -- of the legislative branch of which you were a member, the activities of the parliament whose member you used to be, does your experience confirm that the fear of Serbs were -- was justified and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... looming up. The format of this one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can't ask the question in that way. "... does your experience confirm that the fear of Serbs was justified ..." He is obviously going to say yes, so the evidence would be useless. Move on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did the legislative branch act in those years from 1990 to 1991 when you were a member?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in 1990 constitutional amendments were introduced, and later a new constitution was introduced, bringing a new coat of arms and a new flag and establishing the Latin script as the only official one. It turned out that the five-pointed star, the symbol of anti-fascism was erased from the coat of arms and the crescent and six-pointed star became new symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why do you object to the new coat of arms if we know that the so-called chequerboard was the oldest Croatian coat of arms?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It features already in 18th and 17th century tombstones and other symbols -- sorry, 9th century symbols. That is the best known Croatian coat of arms. But they don't put the chequerboard. They put the crescent and the six-pointed star established by Pavao Vitezovic as a symbol of Iliria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, Mr. Milosevic told us that all of this was about explaining why the Serbs reacted. Can you give me an example of Serb reaction that was caused by this sort of conduct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, normally they reacted -- they reacted even to this coat of arms. When it was adopted, Serb MPs cautioned that the anti-fascist symbol should not be abolished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We want to know about crimes or conduct that could be described as a crime unless it was justified in some way. Now, can you give me an example of Serb reaction of that nature which was caused by this conduct on the part of the legislature, on the general attitude of the Croats towards the Serbs trying to expel them from their land, and so on. What was it that the Serbs did? Give me an example that could be described as criminal conduct as a result of this behaviour of the Croatian authorities. You see, if you can't, then I would be driven to the conclusion that this is tit-for-tat, that this is a case of let's try and prosecute Croatia here and never mind defending the allegations against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Bonomy, the Serb people and the Serb politicians did not give the Croatian authorities a single excuse to act like this, to be erased from the constitution, et cetera. On the contrary, Serb authorities asked for autonomy at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be true but that's not the question I'm asking you. The question I'm asking you is not about the Serbs giving cause, which would be prior behaviour, I'm asking you about subsequent behaviour. What is it -- what other ways in which it is said the Serbs reacted because of this behaviour, because that's what Mr. Milosevic has told us this evidence is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Serbs pointed out these phenomena, either through their MPs or political parties. They opposed what was going on in various ways in 1990 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was very responsible of them, but what we're looking at is conduct that could possibly be described as irresponsible and even criminal unless it was justified. Now, give me an example of that. What was the form in which the Serbs reacted to this attitude, irresponsible attitude of the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Serbs reacted only through their MPs, as far as the legislative branch is concerned. In various gatherings and meetings they also expressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't confine your answers to the legislative branch. Any authoritarian behaviour that you say caused reaction from the Serbs, give me an example. And if you can't, just say so and we'll let Mr. Milosevic explore it a little further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all I know is that Serbs had given no cause. However, they were constantly under attack, both by the legislative and the political authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue, and bear in mind the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, this parliament in which you served, did it acknowledge and accept a single, at least one Serb amendment in the new Croat constitution?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single proposed Serb amendment was accepted in the new constitution. I proposed amendments myself as an MP. I warned that Serbs should not be erased from the constitution, that they had always been an equal people in Croatia for many centuries. However, the parliament did not pay attention to anything of the kind and erased Serbs from the constitution without any explanation given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is about the constitution. But now concerning laws that are adopted based on that constitution, were you faced with any discrimination as an MP? Did you witness any discrimination in those new laws?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many laws were passed by parliament in which the Serbs experienced legal discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How? How did they suffer from legal discrimination? Explain.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they were thrown out of the constitution. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we already heard that about the constitution. I'm asking you about the laws now.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many laws were enacted, such as the law on primary education, basic education, and the Serbs are not mentioned in that law at all. The Serbian language isn't mentioned. All that is mentioned is the Croatian language, which was introduced. So there was total discrimination. And the Serbs understood this, this legal discrimination, as state terror against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, apart from language, was there anything else? What about in the material world? What about discrimination there? For example, the budget, when the budget is passed. Did any discrimination crop up there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the budget for 1990 and 1991, when the budget was passed for the Republic of Croatia, not a single dinar was allocated and earmarked for Serb schools, but it was allocated for tuition in the Croatian language and for the national minority schools; Italian schools, Hungarian schools, Ukrainian schools, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a positive facet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just going back briefly, what language is it that you're speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I speak the Serbian language. I'm speaking Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I see this, all of this evidence really as a kind of background to the charges in the indictment, but you need to appreciate that evidence that the Serbs were discriminated against by Croatia will not provide an answer to the charges in the indictment, but I allow you to lead it because it's almost a part of the res gestae. But I presume you will be bringing evidence that relates to the specific charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that I'll show that. I'll do my best. But I want to say that the charges in the indictment have nothing to do with me, and any normal person would be able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Atlagic, are there any concrete pieces of evidence according to which the Croatian authorities in parliament - we're talking about parliament - incited nationalism, for example? You spoke about nationalism and fascism and so on. Do you have concrete proof and evidence of this being incited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I want to examine the statement that you just made and which you have made before, because I need to be clear as to -- as to what your case is. You say that the charges in the indictment have nothing to do with you and anybody can see that. Well, what, then, are you seeking to establish through the evidence that you are leading?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying to establish the truth because we're talking about a completely distorted picture here of some sort of Serb blame which has been construed. That does not mean at all that certain Serbs did not commit certain crimes, individual crimes. I can't address those, I can't say yes they happened or not because I don't have the facts at my disposal, but certainly I don't exclude the possibility that certain crimes did take place. However, those crimes have absolutely nothing to do with the policy and politics of the Krajina leadership and especially not the policy and politics of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear from Mr. Kay on this matter, because it is an important issue: What is the accused's case? And is he to be allowed to continue to lead evidence which, on the face of it, does not serve any forensic purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The case brought against him on the Croatian indictment has been that this was a background and conflict provoked by the Serbs. If you remember, the Court has gone many times back to the so-called SANU memorandum, which seems to be a document that was never published in an official form but the Prosecution have set great store by the fact that there was Serbian activity that was seeking to make the Serbs the dominant people within Yugoslavia. The accused's case has been to consistently reject that and show that the political and social circumstances in the former Yugoslavia as it was breaking up was in fact a time when the other republics were acting specifically against Serbs. Again, the effect of this evidence has a limited use in terms of the counts on the indictment, and I acknowledge that. What the accused appears to be seeking to do is to try to redress some of the balance in the case. He doesn't know how the Judges are going to be affected by the presentation of the context of the Prosecution case and he's obviously attempting to try and redress that balance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are there paragraphs in the Croatian indictment to which this relates? Because we have found on past occasions that the indictment itself opens up areas for discussion which are not necessarily very relevant in themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The passage that it would be best to go to would be the passage at the end where you have the so-called additional facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that paragraph 100 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 91 -- 84 onwards. And paragraph 103 we have the allegation of Greater Serbia, which has been specifically made against the accused. We all know that the beginnings of this lay with the so-called log revolution, the municipalities, the villages within the Croatian Serbian Krajina where they were resisting the political forces that were taking place within the Republic of Croatia at that time, and the reasons for them taking the steps that they did, and Your Honours have heard evidence about this from several witnesses, the resistance that was taking place by those Serbs to the developments taking place within Croatian society from 1989, 1990, to 1991, in the context of this witness's evidence become the more understandable for that resistance. This was not a resistance to create something in relation to Serbia. This was a movement to protect those Serbian peoples within the Krajina and elsewhere who were resisting unfavourable developments in Croatian society towards them; i.e., this is not a plan that comes from Belgrade or Serbia but is an understandable reaction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you understand -- what do you understand the accused to mean when he says that the charges have nothing do with him and that must be clear to anybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, what took place within the Serbian Krajina of Croatia and elsewhere was not caused by him. These were -- these were not resistance movements that arose as a result of any policy from Belgrade or any direction by him. These were understandable resistance movements to what was happening within Croatian society. So this was born within the Republic of Croatia by those Serbs living there who were able to experience a change in that republic that was alienating them from its society culturally and politically and failing to recognise them as a people within it, and they could see, in the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, that the future for them within this secessionist movement of Croatia was leaving them without any caring government or any government which had any concern for their best interests, welfare, and development, and so the resistance, what happened within Croatia, came about from within. On previous occasions Mr. Milosevic has described this as a civil war, and that is, as I see it, the context in which he's presenting his case on the Croatian indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Came from within and not from without.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or if without, certainly not anything to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in his cross-examination of witnesses within the Prosecution case - I have in mind C-060, C-020, Lazarevic, Slobodan Lazarevic, those witnesses we heard in October 2002 - that was very much along the lines that this was a rebellion from within Croatia for understandable reasons, and this was not something those politicians and leaders from the local society, C-037 and others, may have visited Belgrade, may have met him as part of their continuing search for support and help, but in fact they took their destinies in their own hands, and that is what they were concerned about. Their futures, livelihood and security was something that they had to positively deal with by their own steps because there was no support for a proper humane regard for their development within Croatia, and this politician with his background and from his position was, so to speak, trying to advance the interests of the Serbian people within Croatia entirely unsuccessfully. I hope that assists the Court as I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm still concerned as to whether it's a proper use of the Court's time for Mr. Milosevic to spend the time that he's allocating to himself for Croatia in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it may well be that he's proved sufficiently already the background to his case by the evidence that he has called, and often an advocate has to draw a line in relation to how far they go with a particular line of defence before they move to the next stage, and it may well be that he has proved these facts sufficiently already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Defence admits that there were actually some support or assistance from the Republic of Serbia to the Serb people in Krajina. Then this kind of background material may be relevant, whether the purpose that the support is to help the people defend themselves or to commit crimes. Is that the Defence case? Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As I read the cross-examination of Mr. Milosevic in the Prosecution case, it was clear that he was presenting it on the basis that there were at times necessary the self-defence of people within that territory, that the indictment, which starts in August 1991 in relation to crimes, was in a period when the Yugoslavia was still in existence. Croatia had not seceded from the former Yugoslavia. That came at a much later date, and towards the end of the period of the charges in the indictment which run up to June 1992. The evidence Your Honours have been hearing largely concern, in relation to crimes in Croatia, the period when Croatia itself may be considered not to have been a state, it was still part of the former Yugoslavia. The JNA still would have had responsibilities throughout Yugoslavia in relation to the protection of people within in certain circumstances. And the -- when you look at the evidence called by the Prosecution in relation to the Croatian charges, take Slobodan Lazarevic. Virtually all his evidence was outside the time frame of the indictment. He was dealing with 1993, 1994, 1995, later on in 1992. Very, very small passages of that witness's four days of testimony concerning the role of the DB and the JNA and alleged links between them and the RSK, virtually -- hardly any of that evidence was within the time frame of the indictment. One of the problems Mr. Milosevic has had to face is the presentation of the case against him which did not confine itself to the time frame of the indictment, and it's probably very difficult for an advocate to restrain themselves at times and to take that bold decision, if you like, to put material on one side and just focus on the period where the case lies against them. But I can understand why he may have been misled when one looks at the Prosecution evidence that was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kay, you make a number of very good points, and I understand the relevance in at least a limited way of some of this evidence, but it's linking it to the indictment that -- or the failure to link it to the indictment that makes it of doubtful relevance as far as I'm concerned, because we have here a witness who doesn't know of any incidents that could even be described as self-defence and is telling us about events in the parliament and other circles of authority in Croatia which he now speculates may have caused fear or may have justified fear among the Serbs, but we've had no evidence of actual fear or actual behaviour that results from that. So one has to wonder how that can be relevant to the indictment, and that's the point I've been trying to make. And while I understand the general point you make, it seems to me there's been ample evidence led on the general background and that this is a failure to make a reasonable use of the time that is available to concentrate on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the accused needs to understand he can use the good points he obtained in the Prosecution case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And many of them -- many of them, I may say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he shouldn't underestimate what has actually been gleaned from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And those witnesses I cited, all of which contributed evidence that supported this background to this aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. We have been assisted by Mr. Kay's explanations. It's a little clearer to me what you're trying to do by way of this evidence on background, but always bear in mind the need to relate it to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the starting point here is that certain crimes were committed. Once a civil war breaks out, there are casualties and victims on all sides. That is not something that is contested. But I'm explaining to you that that has nothing to do with Serbia, and you'll be best able to understand all this if you look at paragraph 89, for example, of the Kosovo indictment, which was written before they received instructions to indict me for Croatia and Bosnia, which is quite nonsensical. Here is what it says in paragraph 89: "Slovenia, on the 25th -- on the 25th of June, 1991, Slovenia declared its independence from the SFRY, which led to the outbreak of war. Croatia declared its independence on the 25th of June, leading to fighting." Now, what led to fighting? The proclamation of independence and that declared by armed forces. Look at the following: Bosnia-Herzegovina declared its independence which, after the 6th of April, resulted in a wide-scale war. Now, we're not dealing with Slovenia here, or you're not dealing with Slovenia, and that's not important, but both in the Croatian and Bosnian indictment they wrote themselves what led to war. Once a war breaks out and then somebody kills somebody else, let's see who is responsible for that in Belgrade. It's the greatest nonsense that you can conceive of. Once a war breaks out and somebody kills someone, that's why it's called a war, that's what happens. But the question is what brought about that war, and here they themselves wrote how the war came about. And we're discussing Krajina at the moment. The Serbs exclusively defended themselves, defended themselves in front of their own houses. They didn't go to Zagreb to attack it, they didn't defend Rijeka or whatever, they defended their own homes. They were in front of their own homes until the UN forces came to protect them. And the UN protected areas are zones where the Serbs live. They were the subject of this UN protection. Once the United Nations arrived, that is to say in 1991, they never attacked anybody after that. They didn't even attack anybody before that, they were just defending themselves; that's quite clear. Now, in all this, some crimes had probably been committed. I cannot enter into discussion about all these crimes. That would be nonsensical. I cannot know about them. I am dealing with research now. I cannot investigate as a separate organisation but that -- the situation is quite clear, and they themselves wrote it down in the indictment. Once a war breaks out, of course, then people die, and it's mostly the innocent that lose their lives in a war, that's something that cannot be challenged. Now, that somebody was sent from Serbia to commit a crime, that is quite nonsensical. We assisted Serbs, sent assistance, aid and assistance on all sides. From all of Serbia enterprises, individuals, the state, everyone sent aid and assistance. We received several hundred thousand refugees ourselves, but assistance was never given for the purpose of a crime being committed. How could you give assistance to somebody under jeopardy for them to commit crimes whereas it is them that were under jeopardy, and then to help them commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's nonsense, and that's why I say it's nonsense which any man of reason would be able to see as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Before you continue, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber is of the view that you can deal more expeditiously with these matters, and you should move on to other areas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The points that you have been trying to make, I believe we have heard enough evidence in relation to those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, let us move on now to your actions in connection with this situation which they no longer want us to illustrate. A preliminary question: Did the Croatian parliament do anything to put a stop to these nationalist and fascist speeches in the country?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The parliament did nothing to stop the spread of fascism in Croatia. On the contrary, they encouraged it, either by their actions or by their failure to act. It was more by failure to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you, as MP Marko Atlagic, what did you respond to? Let me help you. In tab 16, we have certain documents that refer to you personally. Explain, please, how you responded, what you responded to, and what you asked for early on. This was 1990, mid-1990. Look at tab 16. Is there a date here? It says the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at the first session of the first multi-party parliament in Croatia - this was in late May, 1990 - I saw nationalism and fascism being revived. I will tell you what this was about. At the first multi-party session, President Tudjman, the president of the republic, Dr. Zarko Domljan, the speaker of parliament, and other leaders of the Republic of Croatia, when they made their inaugural speeches, they let it be known what they wanted to do with the Serbs. They threw out the Serbian people from their definition of the Republic of Croatia. In his inaugural speech, President Tudjman said that the Croatian state was the state of Croatian -- the Croatian people and other inhabitants. Serbs were nowhere mentioned. This first session was of a celebratory nature, so I wasn't able to speak, but I spoke at the second session, held on the 28th and 29th of June, 1990, and put questions as to why they were doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, according to parliamentary procedure, you can respond only by putting questions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say here? There is a document where it says question put by Deputy Marko Atlagic regarding the inaugural speeches of the highest ranking republican officials at the constituent session of the Assembly. This is an official document whereby your question is being passed on. There is only one page of these shorthand notes. I see that the second page is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want him to read it. I just read it in its entirety. You can just tell us in summary form what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't have to read it out, but you are responding to their inaugural speeches and saying that the Serbian name is not mentioned, and you speak of the status of the Serbs. I won't go on to read all of this, but what did you say here?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I warned the parliament at the first working session of the first multi-party parliament that the leaders of the Republic of Croatia, the Assembly, or parliament, and the Executive Board were not complying with the then-valid constitution of the Republic of Croatia when addressing us MPs and other guests by failing to define the Republic of Croatia in the way it's defined in the official constitution. The official constitution said that the Republic of Croatia was the state of the Croats, the state of the Serbs in Croatia, and of ethnic minorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are actually drawing attention to the fact that they are violating the provisions of the still-valid Croatian constitution, Article 1, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I put three questions here. Unfortunately, the other pages have not been kept, but I asked why they were doing this. Was it an involuntary omission, or is it because they didn't like the Serbian people, or is it because they want to expel the Serbs from the constitution? This was actually an indication of their intentions, and later on they actually did precisely this; they threw the Serbs out of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Atlagic. Here we see the document sent to the cabinet by the Croatian parliament, and according to the law you had the right to reply. Did you ever get a reply?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Although under the law I was to receive one. I saw Dr. Tudjman in Varazdin, speaking in Varazdin, I think on Croatian television, and he said that some MPs were putting very unpleasant and inappropriate questions. I never received a written reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before we resume, the question I asked earlier about the constitution of Croatia, I was certainly confused in my own mind at the time the explanation was given. If reference was being made to the explanation that Mr. Kostic gave at the end of cross-examination, that was about the constitution of Bosnia. Was there separately --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think he had both. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff might be able to give you the better detail because she was dealing with it, but our recollection is that he had both, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But did he give us an account from both?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll leave Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he did. He referred to both the constitutions of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In addition to that, he also referred to certain rules, but these rules of procedure or what it was we didn't give to him. We gave him the two constitutions to look at to find the passage where he claimed that was in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just one additional remark. It was not exhibited because we only had the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Milosevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, you raised several MP questions in parliament. Look at tab 17. It says here that the decision of the new parliament at its first constituent session to exclude the Yugoslav national anthem is inappropriate. You are asking the Croatian parliament to distance itself from that. Did you ever get a response to that? What was the response?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a parliamentary session, I raised a question connected to nationalist incidents at a football match between Yugoslavia and the Netherlands at the football stadium in Maksimir. Forty thousand spectators turned their backs when the national anthem of Yugoslavia was played, and they burned the Yugoslav flag. And they also rooted for the Dutch team. So I put a question in parliament, asking that perhaps the decision on excluding the Yugoslav national anthem in its protocol may have had an indirect influence on the events at the Maksimir football stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And my question was did you ever get a reply?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did get a reply in writing from the Executive Committee, or Council, of the parliament to the effect that this was because the football clubs Dinamo and Hajduk did not provide a single player in the Yugoslav national team and that that was the reason for the incidents. And there had been similar incidents at the football match previously played in Zagreb between the Red Star of Belgrade and the Zagreb Dinamo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't follow that last answer. You got a reply from the Executive Committee or the Council of the parliament to the effect that this was because the football clubs and something or the other did not provide a single player in the Yugoslav national team. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's exactly what they said. The spectators were responding because not a single footballer from Zagreb or from Split was playing in the Yugoslav national team. And that was a strange kind of reply which I failed to understand. And that was the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now to move on to a more serious issue, a more difficult question you put, which is in tab 18. Only the second of your questions is mentioned here, and that is: "Is it true that a large group of cadets in the police school in Zagreb sang songs --" read this.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... 'My aunt advised me that all the Serbs should go (I will not say this word) themselves', 'We Croats don't drink wine but the blood of the Serbs from Knin', 'Croatia, our Croatia, you are the country of all the true Ustashas' ..." End of quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you learned that these cadets in the police school were singing that, and you asked that the minister of the interior resign.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked that Minister Boljkovac resign because true dramas were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say true human dramas, as it says here. What kind of human dramas, genuine human dramas were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring primarily to the feelings of the parents of these cadets and the citizens, especially in the Krajina, citizens of Serb ethnicity. This was madness and parents and journalists informed us of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did the minister of the interior respond, the government, the parliament, how did they respond?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received a reply. Their response was silence. I never got a reply to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did this take place? What is the date here?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this took place sometime before -- well, before November 1990. It was in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it happened in October 1990. All right. And what about your response and the question you raised in parliament in tab 19?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In tab 19, there is a question I raised as an MP in parliament in connection with a statement made by the deputy speaker of parliament, Stjepan Sulimanac, who spoke about the Jadovno mass grave where 46.000 Serbs were interred who had been shot, and he said that it should be covered over with concrete. I asked whether the parliament or the government of the Republic of Croatia would distance themselves from this uncivilised and unprecedented barbaric act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where and when did he say this? This is the 3rd of July, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you get any response in this case? This was a speech made by an official.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received a short, written reply that this was Mr. Sulimanac's own personal matter, that it nothing to do with the parliament or the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is there in the question you raised in parliament which we can see in tab 20?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In tab 20 is a question I put at the parliamentary session in connection with ethnic or national cleansing of Serbs from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, which was headed by Mr. Spegelj. I asked whether it was true that on the 17th of October at 1500 hours in the office of the Minister of Defence of Croatia Spegelj 21 employees of the ministry were summoned by Perica Juric, who was the assistant minister of interior affairs, and told that within an hour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within half an hour they were to hand over the keys to their offices and desks and leave their workplaces. I asked whether it was true that there were two Montenegrins, two Croats, and two Serbs there, and what number of Serbs were there, and I asked whether they were drawing up lists of people who were not considered suitable for these jobs and whether this was done according to instructions from President Tudjman. He said: "We did not draw up a party platform for the party but for all of Croatia. We need people who are of good character and who are good employees and that individuals shouldn't hide behind the HDZ platform." This is what he said, President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this before that or is this the first time you learned about this cleansing, as you called it, in parliament?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was ethnic cleansing in the Ministry of Defence. I learned about it in direct contacts with those 21 persons. This was a purge. And they -- they came to me. Why did they come to me? Because I was the only Serb MP who dared raise these issues in parliament. That's why they came to me. And I raised these questions, and then I met them and talked to them. Twenty-one employees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber has heard enough evidence on the questions put by this witness to the parliament. Move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are several more questions raised by him in the parliament --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic. We've heard enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am now saying only for procedural reasons that all these questions raised by him should be exhibited, because these are official records of the Croatian parliament and they concern the witness directly. That is my request to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit them, Mr. Milosevic. Their value is another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence binder will be Exhibit D334.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber hasn't been make orders tab by tab as the exhibits have been looked at. My position is on the extracts, with the exception of tab 13, I think it is, remains, that I would challenge the admissibility of things that are extracts and don't come in a context. It may well be that if they came in context there would be other passage of these articles that I'd like to draw to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just deal with the extracts? There is a difficulty over the volume of translated material and at times he's been told to take extracts and not to use the whole of the material, and so the accused in pointing the Trial Chamber's attention to the point that he wants to make, in my submission, is adopting a good practice for the benefit of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may be an understandable difficulty, Mr. Nice. We'll admit all of them, and we note -- we note the comments made by Mr. Nice as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, who started the armed conflicts in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were started by Croatian paramilitary organisations. That is a well-known fact, common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have an example to give, an example of a fellow MP who was involved in such activities?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in 1990, even my fellow MPs got involved directly on the ground. Among them my fellow MP who later became president of the municipality of Osijek, Branimir Glavas, who in October 1990 distributed a powerful explosive called Vitezit in his municipality. Sometime around the 6th or 7th of October he disarmed a legal police patrol and criminal proceedings were instituted against him. However, already on the 12th October he was appointed by the Municipal Assembly by secret ballot secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence, and believe it or not, it was the Minister of Defence Martin Spegelj who gave his approval for that although the man was under criminal investigation at the time. There were Croat MPs whom I told it is their turn to raise this issue in the parliament, it is up to them rather than to me, and they replied they were afraid for their families. They didn't want to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about how paramilitary formations were set up in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that because I was an MP. The Croatian parliament decided that special units would be organised within the civilian defence, an organisation that is meant to deal with fires and such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they need weapons for dealing with fires?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but they did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did the Croatian government approach this issue?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in July it formed special youth brigades whose task was to protect people's lives and property. Those were the paramilitary organisations. Already in June 1990 they established these paramilitary organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were involved very actively. They organised workshops where training was provided for youth units, and the requirement was that the men should not be older than 27 and that they recruited mainly criminals, people who used to be criminals in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time did you know anything about the reorganisation of the Ministry of the Interior, that is the police in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely at that time there was a reorganisation of the Ministry of the Interior so that public security stations in Serb majority areas were abolished and subordinated to public security stations in Croat majority areas; towns, and villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they put under the jurisdiction of Croat majority areas in all cases?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, including boards. They wanted to disarm police stations from majority Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How was this done in terms of staffing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of August, this announcement was made that people were being recruited. On the 27th of July. The requirements were made clear: They were not to be older than 27, and at this public competition, they recruited these people, these people were given weapons and sent later to Serb villages to organise provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself are from Benkovac. What did it look like there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th, 17th August, a group of men from the public security station in Osijek came to Benkovac to disarm policemen in Benkovac, and they seized a lot of weapons, long and short barrels. The same thing happened later in Petrinja, Dvor Na Uni, and other places. As for Benkovac, the next day, when the people found out that this had happened, they organised a rally before the Municipal Assembly, and they were addressed by the president of the Municipal Assembly, Zdravko Zivkovic. However, the people were so fiery in asking for somebody to be found responsible, and the opposite side was already taking the weapons to Zadar. I addressed the people because the situation was very tense and I calmed the people down. That afternoon the rally resumed at 5.00, when Jovan Raskovic addressed the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to Serb policemen during that reorganisation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dismissed from their jobs. For instance, in Zadar, 17th -- 17 policemen were dismissed in November, and in protest against this move, 130 policemen from Zadar, Benkovac and Obravac [phoen] did not want to work and they were later all dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The police officers in Benkovac, was carrying a long-barrel weapon a normal part of the duty of such police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At that time, policemen did not carry long barrels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where did the police officers in Benkovac get the long-barrel weapons from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the police station there was also the reserve force of the police, and they had that in safekeeping. Not only in Benkovac, but every police station had a reserve of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time did the Croatian Ministry of the Interior -- all this is happening in summer and early autumn 1990, all that you've described?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
