utterances.text: Did the Croatian MUP start opening new police stations in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in end 1990 and early 1991, Croatia started opening new police stations in Serb majority places, and the purpose was to provoke Serbs, to create incidents, because that was what the authorities wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the first armed action that you know about in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 17th of August, in Benkovac. It had to do with that rally. At that time the Ministry of the Interior sent three vehicles full of armed policemen from Korenica. However, people blocked them and they did not reach their destination. On the 15th of February, 1991, there was another major incident in Plitvice, and that is considered to be the first one, although the previous one I described is actually the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were in the focus of those events. Tell us, how did the federal authorities react to the decision of the Croatian government to establish the Home Guards Corps and other paramilitary organisations?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia organised its paramilitaries already on the 9th November 1990, when they elected the commander of the Territorial Defence of Croatia, because they adopted a law then according to which the commander was chosen by the Presidency of Croatia, not the Presidency of the SFRY. However, the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia reversed this decision on the 26th of June, 1991, the decision to establish the Home Guards Corps. And later even the Presidency of Yugoslavia issued an order or, rather, a decision on the 9th of January to disarm all paramilitary formations in Croatia. Croatia, however, ignored it, and we in the parliament were not even informed about it. And then on the 20th of January, the Croatian government asked for a prolongation, for an extension of the deadline for this disarming for 48 hours, and the Presidency asked for it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did the Croatian authorities do then?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instead of disarming them, on the 20th of February, 1991, the Croatian authorities adopted a decision saying that all federal laws were null and void in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did they arm these new formations in the first place, and how did Serbs actually arm themselves and why?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all happening at the time when there were many rallies calling for extermination of Serbs. After that, the new constitution of Croatia was adopted without any Serbs as constituent people, invocations of the past, Ante Starcevic and Mile Budak, dismissals of Serbs, especially from the police and national defence organisations, killings of policemen and Serbs. After all that, Serbs had no choice but to arm themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did they do that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through smuggling of arms. Apart from that, peasants sold their property and cattle in order to buy a rifle. Some of them got weapons from police stations who had provided the weapons normally belonging to reservists to Croatian majority areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the context of what you are describing, what was the situation in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that in Benkovac the situation on the -- between the 16th and the 17th in the evening -- or, rather, a group arrived in some Land Rovers - a type of vehicle - they were armed, and they wanted to take the weapons of the reserve police force, and I said the kind of barrels they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 16th and 17th of August?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And the following day, what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did happen the following day? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the following day, as a sign of protest, the people went in front of the Municipal Assembly building to hold a rally, and then the rally moved to the public security station where they called for the chief of police to be held responsible, and not only the chief but the soldiers, too, for having allowed the weapons to be handed over and the police station disarmed. And in the afternoon hours, there was another rally near Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what happened on that particular day in Korenica, for example? Was there any intervention by the MUP of Croatia there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was precisely from Korenica that the MUP of Croatia sent three armed vehicles of specials. They were armed, to intervene against the people down there. However, the Serbs in Lika set up an obstacle and didn't allow them to intervene. And I spoke about this at one of the parliament sessions at the time, and they said that this was a stage set that was -- that took place somewhere else. And I said, "Gentlemen deputies --" I said this in parliament -- "it is you who are sending transportation vehicles bearing arms against an unarmed people for no reason," and they said that the reason -- the reason they gave was that the public security station had sent in a written request saying that the Serbian Democratic Party would disarm them, allegedly, the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge - and now we're talking about August 1990 - of whether the Yugoslav People's Army intervened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. When the three vehicles were returned in the direction of Korenica, the Croatian MUP then sent three helicopters that were armed against those people down there. However, the army intervened and had the helicopters return to base. So that was how the army stepped in. And I mentioned that once again at a parliamentary session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did the army intervene in armed fashion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just issued an order. Or, rather, they made the helicopters land.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Benkovac previously, Mlinar was wounded. You said you went to visit him. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mlinar was president of the Serbian Democratic Party, a pupil of mine, and as I said, he ended up in hospital, but what was interesting was that this was the 18th of May, 1990, before the first multi-party Assembly went into session. However, the Serbian Democratic Party already at that time after that particular incident froze its relations with the Croatian parliament and thawed them one month later. However, what is interesting to note in connection to this case is that on the 1st of June - and the event happened on the 18th of May - but on the 1st of June the Croatian paper Vjesnik published a statement by the vice-president of the Croatian parliament, Vladimir Seks, saying that Mlinar had inflicted the wound on himself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said about Dr. Raskovic, please. He's going far too fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you're being asked by the interpreter to repeat what you just said and to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. Thank you. I was saying that on the 1st of June, the Croatian paper Vjesnik published information to the effect that Mlinar had inflicted the wound on himself and that this was staged in some way by Dr. Jovan Raskovic and then that he acted it out very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, they claim that Mlinar had wounded himself with the knife, stabbed himself with the knife.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but as I was a deputy and it was my constituency, I put a question to the house, to the Croatian parliament. Twenty days later, 20 days after Vladimir Seks had made that particular statement, and I warned the government that great dramas were being played out on the territory and that ethnic tensions had reached a peak and that I wanted information in connection with the Mlinar incident. So I raised this question officially, I put a question to the house, and asked whether there was a criminal investigation into the affair, and later on the answer I received was that the investigation was still under way, and the vice-president of the Sabor gave this statement on the 1st of June, that everything had been concluded, whereas the answer given to me was on the 15th of July that the investigation was still underway and that the case had not been fully investigated. So there was -- he was caught out telling a lie, or an untruth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether in places where there were no tensions or conflicts there were any attempts to cause tension and conflict; and if so, who did this? Who attempted to do that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the scenario in Krajina was like this: Where there were no tensions, the leadership of the ZNG, Croatian National Guards Corps, were sent to villages where the majority population was Croatian but next to Serb villages, and then provocations would start straight away on the part of their members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have an example of this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Lisine-Ostrovicke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the name?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lisine-Ostrovicke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a village with a hundred per cent Croatian population. On the 14th of July, 1991, the forces of the ZNG arrived, police forces, and near that village is the Serbian village of Ostrovica, with very few inhabitants, and elderly inhabitants at that, and when the police force arrived, the inhabitants, when they came to Lisane-Ostrovicke, they forced them out. They said go away. We don't have any problems with the Serbs. And the answer they received was that the ZNG had been sent by Franjo Tudjman. Very soon after there was shooting in Ostrovica, and that's how the clash started. It's interesting to note that the locals of the village of Lisane who were Croats by ethnicity, because the ZNGs caught a Serb along the motorway from Stradun to Benkovac, the Zenga members caught this man and the Croatian population saved him. They took him to the village and saved him. So these Croats behaved admirably. But the Zengas always said we'll fly in your centres to do what we have to do, so that's how the conflict began, that's how the war began in Dalmatia. And that, in my opinion, was the first conflict, major conflict that broke out in Dalmatia, when these persons started shooting, there was retaliation, and then one thing led to another, and you know how things like that spread. That's how a conflict spreads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you've enumerated rather a lot of events dated back from that time. I'm going to quote point 9, paragraph 9 in the Croatian indictment, where it says that the Serb forces, between August 1991 and June 1992, killed hundreds of civilians and deported some of the survivors. A large number of men, non-Serb males, were held in detention centres mostly in Knin and Benkovac, that is to say in your own municipality. Knin is mentioned here and your own municipality of Benkovac. Can you tell us anything about that? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Benkovac, I know that there was no prison or detention centre at that time in the Benkovac municipality, I don't know about Knin. I have no information about Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again the interpreters are asking you both to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 9 is not the correct reference. I don't know if the accused would like to give us the correct reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I've been trying to find it. Mr. Milosevic, what is the correct reference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I might have made a mistake in giving the paragraph number. But not to dwell on that point, I'll look for it, but the allegations are certainly -- or what I read out was certainly correct. I might have got the paragraph number wrong, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we would like to find it, Mr. Milosevic. It's another instance of sloppy management.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is under the impression, knowing the indictment very well, that what he actually did was to summarise the effect of several paragraphs. Now, I've been looking at the indictment myself this morning again and I certainly don't remember anything in the phraseology or with the phraseology given. Perhaps the accused would like to help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was wondering whether in fact the reference was to paragraph 34, but -- which has the time frame.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't find it now, but this was certainly a quotation that is to be found somewhere in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll come back to this, Mr. Milosevic. I expect you to provide us with the correct reference. Move on in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was about the events that took place in the summer of 1991. However, it's all in your region. In Dalmatia a little earlier. In May in Trogir a meeting was held of the leaders of the HDZ party. Now, was there anything significant that happened in Trogir at the meeting of these HDZ leaders that you knew about at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that on the 5th of May, for example, the 5th of May, in Trogir the president of the republic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, called all the representatives of the HDZ at the meeting from the Dalmatia region, the Municipal Board Presidency, in fact, and the presidents of the municipal Assemblies of the region, of the whole of Dalmatia, and quite simply he issued an order to them. He said that the next day they were to attack the military barracks in Split, and that all water supplies and electricity supplies should be cut off to them. So he just gave them an order as to how they should do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not allowing any further examination on this issue. It is unfair to the Prosecution, not to mention the Chamber. How is the Prosecution to cross-examine without having the correct reference, and what are we to make of it without having the correct reference? Mr. Nice, you do not have to cross-examine on that. I'm not allowing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't have any reference here to any kind of indictment that you're mentioning, Mr. Robinson. My question related to the events at the beginning of May in Trogir - I wasn't referring to the indictment - which he, as a deputy, knows about and that was what he was talking about. Of course that's not in this written submission of Mr. Nice's, because he wouldn't have fared well had he written that down. But we're talking about what happened, what went on, and we're talking about May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, two points: First of all, that last remark is moving towards the kind of remark that is quite unacceptable. The substantial, or substantive point is that the evidence this witness has given, or I know the Court has said I don't have to cross-examine on it, but is unsourced in any event. It's just general evidence with no explanation of source, like a lot of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another area, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Robinson, I think that it is very important, because the witness knows from personal experience. I'll ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know about this meeting in Trogir and the instructions given to block the barracks? That is very important because of the date and because of everything that happened later.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about it because I had communication with my colleagues, deputies from the Croatian parliament. I talked to them. And apart from that, what happened the following day in Split was something that the whole world saw because all the television stations throughout the world broadcast that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about the 6th of May. What happened on the 6th of May?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 6th of May, pursuant to instructions from Mr. Tudjman, a mass of workers from most of the companies and enterprises in Split went to the military district and went to block the barracks, and attack the JNA and the barracks, rather, and cut off water and electricity supplies to the barracks, which is what happened. Officers' cars were damaged and anything that reminded anybody about -- of Yugoslavia was damaged and destroyed, such as the Yugoslav airlines offices, the JAT, but Saso Gesovski, a soldier, was also killed on that occasion and two other soldiers wounded. However, the organisers of that rally strangled a soldier in an armoured car. I think it was a tank. This is something that the whole world saw happening. And the strangler of that soldier was promoted later on to officer rank and in 1991 received a decoration from Tudjman for merit for the people in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there was no tension there in Split between the Serbs and Croats, or was there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serb apartments, as my colleague deputies told me, Serb apartments were marked, especially the apartments of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Serbs' conduct in Split? Was there anything untoward there that could have irritated the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no incidents like that or anything that could irritate the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about this clash on the 6th of May? That clash was between the demonstrators and the army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A clash between the demonstrators and the army, and in front of the Naval Military District building they took down the Yugoslav flag, put up a Croatian flag and a green Muslim flag, I think it was ten metres long. And my deputies from parliament told me later of the details of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Am I understanding you correctly; so in Split were there no -- where there were no conflicts between the Serbs and the Croats a clash broke out between the organised extremists and the army by them laying siege to the Military Naval District's building?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They laid siege to the naval district's building pursuant to Trogir's instructions because he was cross with them. He said they should have done that earlier, but if they hadn't done it earlier, they should do the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the army have -- was there any army activity going on in that naval district?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The army was calmly going about its daily duties. The army did not do anything to provoke anyone. They were in the barracks and went about their daily business, the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say the soldiers were not outside the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the territory of your municipality, which is the closest and which we know about and you can testify about, were there any sabotage or terrorist activity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. In my municipality, on the 31st of July, for example, in Ceranje Donje village, there was a sabotage terrorist group led by Miro Barisic, a well-known terrorist who had killed Ambassador Rolovic in Stockholm in 1971, and two other men as well who set mines to the surrounding area and a church courtyard. Why a church courtyard on the 1st of July? Because on the 2nd of August there was a village fair that was to be conducted in that courtyard and in that area and that would have led to destruction; however, the shepherds that tended to the sheep saw these armed people doing something in the fields around the church and they reported this to the Ministry of the Interior and Benkovac and then the group was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the name of the person you say was a well-known terrorist who had killed the ambassador? And we don't have the name of the ambassador in Stockholm in 1971.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the terrorist was Miro Barisic, and the name of the ambassador was Rolovic. He was killed in Stockholm. He was brought to Croatia in 1971. That was when the ambassador was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So he was the Yugoslav ambassador, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a Yugoslav ambassador in Stockholm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was this person tried for the killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware whether he was ever arrested but in the early 1990s he was invited by the authorities and he did what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your basis for saying that he killed this ambassador?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basis is I remember it. It was a notorious fact. The whole world knew it. All of Yugoslavia knew it. It's common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, he did not deny it himself. He boasted about having killed the Yugoslav ambassador, because he was a member of the Ustasha movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say he was never arrested? In Yugoslavia or in Stockholm?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, he wasn't, but I can't assert that. He was a member of the Ustasha formations that the witness is talking about, and that's beyond doubt. He was the murderer of the late Ambassador Rolovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could add, in connection with Barisic, that he had called me on the telephone for five months, disturbing me. He would call me up on the phone and curse at me and insult me because of the issues I raised and the questions I put in parliament as an MP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is Barisic still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he isn't. He was one of the three liquidated on the 31st of July. The entire sabotage terrorist group was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By employees of the Ministry of the Interior of the municipality of Benkovac after they received a report from some shepherdesses guarding sheep. They said they saw some people acting suspiciously in the vineyards and they responded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you the reference. It's paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you whether you know anything about this. It says here: "Serb forces --" and that refers to November 1991, that's a little later in the year, after these events that you've been talking about. "In November 1991, Serb forces comprised of JNA and TO units and Martic's Police attacked the village of Skabrnja near Zadar. On the 18th of November, 1991, the Serb forces entered Skabrnja. Moving from house to house, they killed at least 38 non-Serb civilians ..." and so on and so forth. Do you know anything about the events in Skabrnja? What was this about and how did this occur?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him first provide the basis for any knowledge that he has about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this near your village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Skabrnja is a large village bordering on my municipality of Benkovac. It's on the border between Zadar municipality and Benkovac municipality. What I know about the events in Skabrnja is the following: In Skabrnja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, how would you have received this information? Presumably you were -- you were not there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received information from a person whom I felt to be well-informed in view of his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that person was?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I move that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, what did you learn about this event? I quoted the Serb forces comprising the JNA and TO units and Martic's Police attacking Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that there were Croatian military units, that is Croatian policemen, stationed in Skabrnja, that they provoked the villagers in the neighbouring village on a daily basis, in the neighbouring villages of Biljana Donja, Zagrad, and from a place called Nadinska Kosa, which is an elevation in Skabrnja, they constantly fired into this village of Zagrad where there was a Serbian population, and one person, called Nenad Kuzet, I think, was slaughtered. He had his throat cut and he was stabbed with a knife. He died. And there was another civilian, his last name was Strbac, I don't remember his first name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Zagrad or Zadar?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it Zagrad or Zadar? The indictment refers to Zadar, Z-a-d-a-r. Is that the same place or a different place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zadar is the name of the municipality but a village near Skabrnja is called Zagra, Z-a-g-r-a. It's a small hamlet. The paramilitary forces were provoking on a daily basis, and they even ambushed and killed a lieutenant, I think his name was Stefanovic, and two other soldiers. The paramilitary forces were shelling Biljana Donja, and even Benkovac, on a daily basis, as well as Zemunik airport, the village of Zemunik, and a number of other villages with a majority Serb population. After the soldiers were killed, two soldiers who were ambushed, there was an action, and then what happened happened. What I know is that when the conflicts broke out, the civilian population was brought to Benkovac municipality by the Red Cross, and part of them remained, according to what I heard. In fact, the Croatian intelligence service would not allow some of the civilians to retreat, to withdraw, and the ZNG were using them as a human shield. Of course, they were killed. Of course a certain number of civilians were killed. I don't know exactly how many, but I did hear that a certain number of civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, you said after the soldiers were killed two soldiers who were ambushed, there was an action, and then what happened happened. Could you tell us more in detail about that action, about what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I know, after the lieutenant and two other soldiers were killed, there was an armed clash. In that clash, the Serb forces advanced, and the civilian population was withdrawn through the Red Cross, and then there was an armed conflict in the village and some civilians were killed, as far as I know. That's the information I have. But these civilians were being used by the ZNG as a human shield. That's how they got killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Atlagic, you mentioned -- you used the term "Serb forces." In that clash, the Serb forces advanced and the civilian population was withdrawn. How did the Serb forces consist of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the Territorial Defence and, as the JNA had also been attacked, I assume there were some individuals from the JNA, because they were acting, that is the JNA, was between those villages, trying to prevent bloodshed. But when the ZNG attacked those three and killed them, then a conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were the police members also included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, but I can't say with certainty, that the Ministry of the Interior did participate as part of the TO. It was all the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have difficulty with the idea of your assumption that there were some individuals from the JNA. Do you mean people from the army running loose and wild or do you mean people in the army under the control of their superior officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA was under control then, but according to what I know, they were very upset because three soldiers were ambushed and killed, and also those villages were being shelled on a daily basis, and so a conflict erupted, and when there's a conflict, there's a general situation that's difficult to keep under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, let's clarify this a little bit further. You said that from that village in which the conflict took place, that is Skabrnja, the civilians were taken to Benkovac by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them had been taken care of by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did it happen, then, that a number of civilians remained in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said previously in my evidence that the Croatian intelligence service stopped a number of them and used them as a human shield, facing Serbs, and let a number of them die to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please remind me what evidence the Prosecution led on this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite a lot of evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's quite a lot of evidence. I'll be dealing with it in cross-examination. It comes from a range of exhibits where some witnesses - I'm just myself reminding myself on which is, if any, the lead live witness on the topic - but you'll find the documents are pretty exhaustive of the detail. The source of the documents. And the source of the documents we'll have a look at in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you had -- you had witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Live witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all there was hearsay evidence, as it were, or summary evidence from Mr. Babic, and we have victims as well, but I'll point them to you in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic, please continue. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, I'm not quite sure that I followed. You explained that civilians from Skabrnja were transferred to Benkovac by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, a number of them remained in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you explained that from Skabrnja somebody shot at all those surrounding villages, including Zemunik air field.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a number of civilians were killed. You mentioned somebody named Strbac and a man called Kuzet. That was before or after the shooting in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think it was before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that lieutenant and two soldiers were killed before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then the conflict in Skabrnja followed.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any other report or information that you gained? Because it says here in the indictment that Serb forces went from house to house, killed them at home, in the streets, et cetera. Do you have any more information?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you know then about it? Why did the conflict in Skabrnja happen? Just what you said or there was some other reason as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I have described. That was the main reason why the Croatian paramilitary forces kept provoking the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did the army do close to your municipality, Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They acted as a buffer zone, in this case between Skabrnja and Donja Biljana. They were there to prevent a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can just interrupt to give you a better answer to your previous question. Apart from documents which we'll look at later, two of the eyewitnesses, both I think 92 bis, one a deceased witness, Marko Miljanic, and Bosko Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all that you have been describing, killings of civilians, ambushes of two soldiers and constant shelling from Skabrnja, all those constituted the reason for the ensuing conflict in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of forces of the Home Guards Corps were in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about their size or strength but I know they were strong, rather strong. That's the kind of information I had, based on those day and night shellings and provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that's all you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no other knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- let me just have a look here. Do you know of a village called Bruska and a hamlet Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are in my municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you know about Bruska village and Marinovic hamlet, I will read to you from paragraph 48 of the indictment. "On 21st December, 1991, Serb forces, in particular members of Martic's police, entered the village of Bruska and the hamlet of Marinovic where they killed ten civilians, among them nine Croats. The names of the victims ..." et cetera, et cetera. The annex is further on. So do you know anything about this incident? Let me remind you: The 21st of December, 1991. You say it's a village in your municipality.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know about those events. It's very difficult for me to speak about the locals of Bruska village because I have emotional ties with that village and with Marinovic hamlet. My extended family has ties with them, and my brothers used to work there and were friends with some of those people. This crime was committed by a villain, obviously, and my knowledge is that nine Croats and one Serb were killed. My information is that this was done by illegal groups from the neighbouring village. The neighbouring village is called Medvedja. It has a mixed Serb-Croat population. I also had information that these persons had been in some sort of physical contact even prior to this conflict, before these nine lovely people, Croat people were killed. I think, in fact from what I know, these were irregular groups from the neighbouring village called Medvedja. After that, I believe 12, 13 Croats remained in Bruska. The rest moved out. And the remaining 12 or 13 locals from Bruska were constantly in trouble during the conflict in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they remained?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, what is the source of your information on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source of my information was my position as an MP, which gave me access to certain services who had insight into the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That tells me nothing. Who is the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certain persons. Certain persons who had -- were able to have precise information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you not going to tell me any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you that in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I wanted to clarify that the -- the evidence on which you do not have to cross-examine is that which relates to the wrong information given by the accused about paragraph 9 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't relate to the evidence that he adduced immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness's position on the identification of this source of information is the same as the last time, may that information be given now in whatever terms the Court is content to receive it so that the Prosecution may be more assisted in its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will have to go into private session. Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in public session or in private session, what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No need. I don't need private session, Mr. Robinson. I just want to tell you that if I continue to feel the way I'm feeling now, because I have this thundering noise in my head, I'm not quite sure I'll be able to continue examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, then, we should perhaps have the doctor here examine you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll instruct the court deputy to see that the accused is examined by the Tribunal's doctor. And report to us before the end of the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have been seen by the Tribunal's doctor. The Tribunal's doctor has reported to us. I understand that you are ready to continue. Should you have any problems, you should bring that to our attention. In the meantime, I will instruct the Registrar, through the court deputy, to ensure that you are examined by an appropriate specialist this afternoon. How much longer would you be spending with this witness anyhow? You have spent just about -- a little over four hours so far.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I cannot continue with the examination of this witness. I really don't feel well. But for the record, and I wish to tell you, too, you can consider that I have completed my examination-in-chief so the other side may feel free to examine him, and I thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just let me inquire from you whether in the rest of the examination that you had planned, did you intend to raise with the witness other paragraphs of the indictment, such as paragraph 45 and 48, which deal with actual incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, 45, Mr. Robinson, is Skabrnja, and I asked questions about Skabrnja. As for 48, that's Bruska. I asked him something about Bruska, and as far as I understood it, he answered my questions related to Bruska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I wanted to find out was whether you intended to lead additional evidence in relation to other paragraphs that allege particular incidents in particular villages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot check that out now, but I think that having said what I've said is enough for you. Having completed my examination-in-chief, I cannot continue, and Mr. Nice can conduct his cross-examination if he wishes to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you should be in a position to tell me whether you have other evidence to lead similar to the kind of evidence that you led in relation to the villages that were allegedly attacked by Serb forces in paragraphs 45 and 48. That's a simple question, and I need to know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I've understood you now, because you mentioned paragraph 45 and 48. No, I have no other paragraphs of that kind. And there are none, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In that event, then, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go into private session just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. Into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout your evidence you have had in front of you and have been turning the pages of some notes that you said you were happy for the Court to inspect. May they be made available to the Prosecution, please, Mr. Atlagic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also, as I see, being having your own volume of exhibits. Mr. Nort, please. You've also got your own volume of exhibits which has got handwritten annotations on it. Have you written handwritten annotations on the exhibits themselves?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I put annotations and it's my handwriting. You can take a look at them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we do that over the break and have a look at the bundle of exhibits then, please, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Have you tried to give here a fair picture of the history of events in Croatia, Mr. Atlagic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I have tried to give an objective picture, but not fully because I wasn't able to do so, allowed to do so in full, to present things in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one question because you've spoken -- although you know the Benkovac area well, for obvious reasons, you've spoken much more broadly than that, but what crimes were committed by Serb forces on the territory of Croatia in 1990 and 1991? Or do you say none were? None was, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that there were no crimes. There were crimes in 1991 and both sides. That's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... since you've spoken so broadly, what crimes, please, were committed by Serb forces on the territory of Croatia, and then we'll explore your sources of knowledge. So, please, what crimes?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones I know about -- well, a case that happened in Bruska, my municipality, and the neighbouring municipality of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... forces, were they? That's the question I asked you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was perpetrated by Serb forces in Skabrnja. I said that the Croatian intelligence service put forward these civilians in front of the Serb forces as a human shield, which means that they placed them there, placed them in front of themselves when going to battle. Now, as for Bruska, I said that my knowledge tells me that -- my information comes from the neighbouring village, populated by the Serbs and Croats, and that before the war those two sides were in some physical --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You haven't so far as I know, although questioned a little bit by the Bench, explained these as offences by Serb forces. In the interests of a fair picture, I want you to tell us, please, what offences on Croatia were committed by Serb forces, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the territory of the area I'm testifying about, I don't know that the Serb forces committed any crimes in 1990, the beginning of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the beginning of 1991 too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your evidence, you tell us a fair depiction of events involves no offences committed by Serb forces to your knowledge at any stage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he did say in the area that he's testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the area you're testifying about, do you disavow any knowledge of anything beyond Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have general knowledge. It's not true that I haven't got any. I have general knowledge. I was a deputy, after all, an MP, so I have general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You lived in Benkovac, what, from -- right the way through from 1990 to 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You travelled throughout the area of the RSK throughout that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part I did but not all over the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I may come back to this question of your state of knowledge and whether you were trying to give a fair picture a little later on. Let's move forward. As a level of politician where you were, do you -- are you in a position to accept - just help us with this - that when both Slovenia and Croatia left it was with the effective assent and understanding of this accused, or is that something that's frankly outside your level of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can help you, but -- and I wanted to say during the examination-in-chief but wasn't allowed to do so, that Croatia and Slovenia left forcibly, and I warned at the 14th LCY Congress as a delegate to the 14th, and also the 11th Congress of the League of Communists of Croatia too --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have had evidence from intercepts of discussions between this accused and Karadzic where he explains his expectations for the departure of both Slovenia and Croatia. Exhibit 613, tabs 9 and 15. At your level of being a politician, do you know anything one way or another about the true intentions of this accused to see the departure of Slovenia and Croatia from the Federal Republic of the former Yugoslavia? Or is that better left for him and people at his level?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know about their intentions. I know that the accused strove for Yugoslavia as an integral territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to 1990, just one other question. We've heard, I think, from Milan Babic that as long ago -- not as long ago but even in 1989 Knin was a hotbed of Serb nationalists. I think he may have said many of them drawn from the ranks of the unemployed. Do you know enough about Knin to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from that period, that is to say 1989, that was when the Communist Party of Yugoslavia was in power. And as far as I know, from that time I didn't know any nationalist excessive behaviour in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No reason to doubt what Milan Babic said on matters within his area of knowledge, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that Milan Babic is competent to speak about that period because Milan Babic was a delegate at the 11th Congress of the League of Communists of Croatia together with me and he sat next to me, and I got up to speak about burgeoning nationalism and issued warnings to the Croatian authorities at the time, and Milan Babic kept quiet, he didn't fight against nationalism. He was an anonymous person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you won't answer my question, I'll move on. In my 1990 --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, would you make your question clearer, then. Once again, please, may I hear it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In January 1990, at the 14th Congress of the Communist Party, Slovenia delegates walked out. You presumably were there.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And we know that the Croatian delegation walked out as well. Did you walk out?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the Croatian delegation left but I didn't. I -- no. No. I stayed on until the end for the final session. I, Boro Mikelic -- Boro Mikelic, and five or six others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your orientation as early as January 1990 was already to favour the Serbs over and above the interests of the Republic of Croatia of which you were a delegate.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's your insinuation. I was on the side of Yugoslavia because the Congress was of a Yugoslavia orientation. So already in 1989 and 1988 there were nationalists rampant, and I wrote letters before that. At the 11th Congress I was one of the rare Croatian communists drawing attention to what was happening. So Croatia left the Congress because the League of Communists of Croatia wanted to secede from the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and wanted to have Croatia secede from Yugoslavia. That was as clear as day, and that was clear to us deputies at the time and delegates to the Congress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. At that 14th LCY Congress I submitted a report and warned about what was happening on the territory of Slovenia and Croatia. I provided an analysis for Slovenia according to which 254 - and you can look at the transcripts from that session --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... time is -- You made an interesting observation this morning when dealing with the legislation in the Croatian parliament how none of the amendments proposed by the Serbs was accepted and that this overbearing attitude of the Croatian parliament was one of the causes of difficulty. Going back, please, to the 14th Congress, you will recall that the Slovenians have made it clear, and we've had President Kucan here, made it clear that they came to that Congress with number of amendments that would have enabled the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia to continue but that each and every one of those amendments was voted down by the Serb side in exactly the same way as you now say the Croats voted down Serb amendments in their parliament. President Kucan is right about that, isn't he? There was a complete Serb determination to crush Slovenes' attempt change the position in a way that would have enabled you to go forward.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Those are not the correct pieces of information. You can't link the 14th LCY or LC Congress of Croatia with what was going on in the parliament of Croatia. As for the 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia when it comes to Slovenia, I published the Mladina newspaper and quoted 250 instances of attacks against the Yugoslav army. At the time in Slovenia what was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm going to ask you to listen to the question, please. You made a point this morning about the effect of one over-strong side resisting completely proposals for amendments of another side. I'm asking you to accept, if it be the case, that President Kucan's explanation that that was what happened at the 14th extraordinary Congress is accurate. He is accurate, isn't he? They came with proposals and the Serb side voted every one down. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't agree with Kucan's proposals, and it wasn't the way he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you'd like tell us, then, one of the proposals that the Slovenes brought to take matters forward that was passed by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, and it's difficult for me to remember all the details, but all Slovenia's proposals were aimed at breaking up the League of Communists of Yugoslavia as one united organisation, and in a way they were putting forward proposals to give them an alibi to leave the Congress so that later on Slovenia could leave Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to press further with that question. Let's move on to the next thing chronologically because the party of the SDS was formed in February 1990, and its first chairman was Jovan Raskovic, of whom you've referred, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date because I wasn't a member of the SDS at the time, but I do know that the president was Dr. Jovan Raskovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now -- look at tab 2, please. This party that was to become so influential, led by a man Jovan Raskovic, at this time was putting out extreme propaganda, wasn't it? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which propaganda you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have a look --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did. I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at a document, then, please. It's already an exhibit. Exhibit 446, tab 50. You've drawn to the Court's attention the bad things that you've said have been said by the Croats and, as you appreciate, we have no interest in the Office of the Prosecutor to defend the Croats from the things that they did that were bad or unhelpful or wrong or criminal, not -- not our interest at all. Let's actually see what was happening on the other side. This is Jovan Raskovic in 1990, in a book we've hopefully prepared an adequate passage for context, and these are the sort of things that were being said in 1990, and I read: "The Ustasha movement is also a rational delirium. Already in 1940 when Ustashas were planning the destruction of the Serbs, they made exact geography of all the pits on the territory in the Independent State of Croatia. Not only did they do this but they calculated the dimensions of the pits and determined how many bodies of children and women would fit in each pit. In that way they knew exactly what and how much they could 'do.' The delirium of the slaughter and genocide that took place in 1941 against the Serb people was a rational delirium, and that is why it had such an epochally high 'score.' "The delirium of the Mass Movement in Croatia in the 1970s had rational programmes but it was stopped on the political level. If it had not been stopped on that level, the delirium would have been realised and would have become a murderous delirium. It would have been murderous because it was anti-Serb, genocidal - and it was stopped ..." Just pausing there, do you, looking back, recognise that to be publishing articles like that in 1990 could have an adverse effect on the development of relations between Croats and Serbs? Because this comes from the Serb side, you see. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't accept that, because this was taught in textbooks in primary schools and secondary schools, and what Dr. Raskovic writes in this book is nothing new. The Serbs and Croats knew that from their textbooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, next page, please. The next page, the last passage of this I want to look at, one of the very few propaganda documents or publicity documents that we'll consider. Here is another passage from the same book and it reads, a third of the way down the page: "The nation in displacement, in migration, is always subject to suffering. Suffering of the Serbs was a rule of history. The only thing that has been happening to the Serbs from the Battle of Kosovo until the present time was a huge suffering. Only God's justice saved the Serbs from annihilation, and from complete disappearance of the Serb name. In every century, hundreds of thousands or millions of the best among the Serbs dedicated to their faith and nation were paying their dedication with their lives. The Serb nation has been undergoing destruction for six centuries." And these last -- first two sentences of the next paragraph: "Today, there are not many living Serbs, and there are too many dead Serbs. The dead Serbs, whose energy has not been transformed into dust and ashes, because the energy is eternal, are helping today the living Serbs to restore their spiritual, cultural, and national entity." Now, those are the expressions advanced by the leader of the SDS in the RSK. Do you agree with those expressions of views? Sorry, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the expressions advanced, if you read this, the book by Dr. Jovan Raskovic, then on the whole they are true and correct in the sense that the Serbs really did suffer in many wars. They suffered in many wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... want to know a little bit more --

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through no fault of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I want, please, do you adopt, do you think these are reasonable views to hold of the position of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the position of the Serbs from the Battle of Kosovo up to 1990 was very difficult because of the historical circumstances in which they lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is a theme that I'm going to try and ask you to deal with as we run through the events that you've dealt with, and the theme is this: The Serbs make much of their suffering, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every man in the world is susceptible to his suffering. I don't think that the Serbs make much of their suffering. Every person of culture in the world would do the same. I assume it's one's ability to see one's pain and suffering because of one's future, in order to avoid --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- suffering in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The second part of my question to you is this: Between the period of time between 1990 and 1992 -- 1995, under guise of their suffering, the Serbs in your area were seeking to obtain and for a time did obtain that to which they were not entitled, namely the independence or near independence of their Serb units from Croatia. They did it under cover of their suffering which they advanced and used to generate emotion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What you are trying to say, the Serbs did not get anything that wasn't their due. They had the same rights until 1990 as the Croats had. As soon as the Croats broke off, well, the Serbs had the right to say who they were going to live with, regardless of the suffering. So it was equal rights. It was a question of equal rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, if the Chamber is obliged to rise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- I ask one last question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this still your view, because you've developed since the 1990s - and we'll follow your development - but is this still your view, that in coming here to this Tribunal, you will have one of your three privileges, one of which was to defend -- that you went with weapons to defend the Republic of Serbian Krajina as a university professor; the second of which was that you met Vojislav Seselj in Western Serb areas; and the third is that you'll be able to tell the truth about the Republic of the Serbian Krajina? Is that still your view?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it is very rare that in anybody's -- in the life of any man you have the chance to defend your own people. Not everybody can do that. So it is a privilege to defend one's own people when the -- that people has been attacked by -- have been attacked by someone. The second privilege is, and I truly believe that it is a privilege, to meet Vojislav Seselj as the president of a political party and a universal -- a university professor. And the third privilege, would you repeat that, please, what was that one that you mentioned, my third privilege?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, I'll deal with that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that privilege is one, too, to tell the truth as I see it and as I experienced it and as it truly is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to adjourn now, but I just remind the court deputy of the instruction that I have given for the Registrar to arrange to have Mr. Milosevic examined by a doctor competent to deal with his complaints, and that should be done this afternoon and a report submitted to the Chamber by tomorrow or in any event at the earliest possible time. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
